source.title: Exact Gap between Generalization Error and Uniform Convergence in Random Feature Models
source.authors: Zi-Tong Yang; Yu Bai; Song Mei

record.tranche_reason: The paper analytically studies generalization error in a nonlinear random feature model and reports how it changes with model size, testing the post-interpolation size trend in V4. It does not reproduce the original deep-network sweep or establish the full fall-rise-fall curve.
record.gate_note: The paper cites double descent in prior work and says random feature models exhibit similar properties, but those cited findings are not rows. Its own results analyze test risk over an overparameterized regime; the uniform-convergence quantities are not test-error results. The sample-size risk trends are recorded as related findings, but they are not near the interpolation threshold.
record.test_reason: The paper studies uniform-convergence bounds (U, T) for random feature regression. The test-risk curve R comes from Mei & Montanari (2019): the authors 'adopt' its closed-form formula and use it as the benchmark the bounds are compared against. Their own results are the U and T asymptotics. The R-versus-features evaluation (Fig. 4) covers only ψ1 ≥ 2 > ψ2 = 1.5, so it shows no peak and no crossing of the threshold. It re-evaluates a formula whose source already established double descent in this model, rather than testing any version anew. Double descent is mentioned only as a cited property of random feature models.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely right. The main conclusion is that uniform convergence over interpolators gives a non-trivial bound where classical uniform convergence is vacuous with label noise, and that in the noiseless case both bounds have worse sample-complexity rates than the true risk. The feature-count point is that U, T and R all decay to their limits at rate 1/ψ1, so both bounds correctly predict the risk decreasing with more features. R itself is taken from Mei & Montanari's formula, not derived anew.
record.recipe_differences: The study derives asymptotic results for nonlinear random feature regression and compares uniform-convergence quantities with minimum-norm interpolator risk; it does not use the original deep-network model-size, epoch, or near-threshold data sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported risk trends differ by noise setting: the noiseless and noisy kernel-regime excess risks have different sample-size power laws. The feature-count result is stated for fixed sample ratio and noise level.

fits_no_version.finding: Classical uniform convergence over a norm ball grows as ψ2^{1/2} with noisy labels, so it is vacuous. Uniform convergence over interpolators stays O(1), and in the noiseless case decays as ψ2⁻¹ versus risk ψ2⁻².
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For min-norm interpolators in random feature models, uniform convergence restricted to interpolators gives a non-vacuous bound where classical uniform convergence fails, but with a sample-complexity gap from the true risk.

fits_no_version.finding: In the kernel limit, min-norm interpolator risk decays with sample size, at rate ψ2⁻² noiseless and ψ2⁻¹ (excess) noisy; these rates come from a cited formula.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In the random feature kernel regime, interpolator excess risk decays with sample size at a rate set by label noise.

record.problems: The risk trends are asymptotic and restricted to specified random feature settings; the feature-count analysis is overparameterized and does not characterize the curve through the interpolation threshold. The paper states technical assumptions that it believes may be provable under more natural conditions but defers their proof.
record.rows_left_out: No reported test-risk rows were omitted. Uniform-convergence values and cited results were excluded because they are not test-error findings from the study.

untested.parts: No sample sweep near the interpolation threshold; the sample-size results are all in the ψ1→∞ kernel limit.
No independent test. The only post-threshold risk decrease is a re-plot of the Mei & Montanari formula over ψ1>ψ2, without the peak or the underparameterized side.
No effective-complexity measure predicting peak location.
Noisy and noiseless rates are compared only in the kernel limit. Peak height, multiple peaks and regularization removing the peak are not examined.

record.verdict_notes: The record's 'tests/T2' and its V4 'supports' label are not justified. The only risk-versus-capacity evidence is the authors' numerical evaluation of a previously published closed-form risk (Mei & Montanari 2019, arXiv:1908.05355), restricted to the overparameterized side. Mei & Montanari is the study that actually tests V4 in random features. The power laws are inferred from log-log linear fits to analytic formulas. The Figure 2 simulations (N=500, n=300, d=200) check U and T, not test risk versus size.

versions.untested_parts: No deep-network model-size sweep or test-error peak near the training-set interpolation size.
The sample-size analysis is in the kernel or large-sample regime, not near a sample-size interpolation threshold.
Tests only the decrease in risk as feature count grows in the overparameterized setting; does not test the initial descent, peak, or behavior across the interpolation threshold.
No single effective-complexity measure is proposed and tested as predicting peak locations across axes.
Compares noisy and noiseless risk scaling, but does not test whether noise drives a peak, whether peaks split, or whether optimally tuned regularization removes a peak.
Does not recount complexity using an effective parameter number or test whether that turns a second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: random feature regression model
rows.size_stated: ψ1 = lim N/d, the number of features per dimension
rows.operation_detail: Analyzes the minimum-norm interpolator's risk as the number of features increases in the finite-width regime.

conditions.value: overparameterized; the paper describes large ψ1 as heavily overparameterized

rows.measure: Minimum-norm interpolator generalization error R(ψ1, ψ2)
rows.note: The paper reports this inferred asymptotic power law for fixed ψ2, noise level, and norm level; Figure 4 illustrates the setting.
rows.check: R(ψ1,ψ2) is Mei & Montanari's formula, evaluated numerically, not a new result. The ψ1⁻¹ rate is a linear fit on a log-log plot over ψ1 from 2 to 1024 at ψ2=1.5 and τ²=0.1. It shows only monotone decrease above the interpolation threshold, with no peak or fall-rise-fall shape. It is a re-evaluation of a cited result, so it should not ground a verdict.

rows.subject: random feature regression model, kernel regime
rows.operation_detail: Analyzes minimum-norm interpolator risk as sample size grows in the noiseless setting.
rows.note: This is a sample-size trend in the kernel regime, not a test near a sample-size interpolation threshold.
rows.check: Kernel-limit (ψ1→∞) sample-size rate, also taken from Mei & Montanari's R formula. It is not near any sample-size interpolation threshold, so it does not bear on V3.

rows.subject: random feature regression model, kernel regime
rows.operation_detail: Analyzes excess minimum-norm interpolator risk as sample size grows in the noisy setting.
rows.measure: Excess generalization error R∞(ψ2; τ²) − τ²
rows.note: This is a sample-size trend in the kernel regime, not a test near a sample-size interpolation threshold.
rows.check: Kernel-limit excess-risk rate in the large-ψ2 regime, from the same cited formula. It has no bearing on V3 or V6, since there is no peak or threshold region.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.condition: Overparameterized random feature regression, with ψ2 = 1.5 and τ² = 0.1 in the illustrated setting
reader_labels.reason: Risk approaches its kernel-limit value with a decaying feature-count correction, consistent with improvement as capacity grows in the tested overparameterized regime (r1).
